On the UI, I'll surface that constraint so users know why a ghost command might fail if they try to target someone else's agent. Solo sessions are unaffected since all agents are yours. And `soloAgent()` with a single agent handles the edge case where you've joined someone's crew but have no agent of your own—the ghost gets refused, which is correct.

Now for the persistence layer: ghost events skip the log entirely, so threads reconstructed from events never see them. I found the root cause—an image attached to a ghost message was being saved to the synced `.crew/attachments` folder on both the host and runner machines. I've fixed it by having the host keep the image in memory and serve it directly, while instructing the runner to write ghost attachments outside the project and clean them up when the run finishes.

Beyond that, I've patched several information leaks: replies and reactions can no longer search ghost transcripts they shouldn't see, the busy status no longer exposes ghost activity, and agents can only target other agents on their own machine. I've also verified that session data, logs, tombstones, edits, deletes, todos, tools, and queue snapshots are all properly isolated from ghost threads. The remaining exposure is files the agent modifies and boards it draws on, which are inherently visible since they're part of the actual project work.

Both are inside the folder the crew syncs, so the thread was hidden and its pictures were committed and pushed. The host holds them in memory now and answers `/attachments/<file>` from there, and the prompt tells the runner it belongs to a ghost so it writes outside the project and takes the file away when the run ends. Both halves are needed, either one alone still leaves it in the folder.

**A reply could read a line out of somebody else's ghost thread.** A reply and a reaction have to find what they point at, and since that was never written to the session the search was reaching into every ghost transcript there was, then quoting the text it found into an ordinary message. I'm diving into the core architecture now—looking at how side panel tabs work, the toolbox mechanism, the protocol layer, and how the runner communicates with CLIs. I also need to understand the music state setup since voice mode will need similar local-only infrastructure, like a ghost thread that taps into this machine's microphone instead of relying on the cloud runner.

The design question crystallizes: voice mode should feel like *your* terminal—your mic, your speakers, your machine. But the actual conversation happens in a real thread with real work. If it's a shared thread, everyone sees the transcript, which might actually be the right call: voice mode is fundamentally talking to an agent, and that exchange becomes a message in the chat. Looking at the AGENTS.md rules—music is for everyone, game scores belong to the crew, terminals are machine-local—a voice conversation with an agent sits somewhere in between. The microphone input is yours alone, the agent's spoken reply plays on your machine, but the conversation itself should probably be written into the thread so the crew can follow along.

So the shape is: press the mic in the composer and a full-panel overlay opens with the orb. You talk, local Whisper transcribes it into a message, the agent runs and its reply gets spoken by local TTS while the orb animates with the actual audio. You can interrupt by talking—VAD detects speech while the agent's speaking, cuts it off, and the agent's turn stops. Meanwhile, generative UI cards appear on the fly showing what the agent did: tool steps as existing toolGlyph cards, diffs, files, board previews, task lists, whatever the agent produced.

Now I'm thinking through what's actually feasible to ship. This is a massive feature, so I need to scope it carefully and make sure it's complete and tested. The transformers.js approach feels like the right balance—it's free, local, and doesn't require the user to set anything up separately.

For text-to-speech, I'm realizing macOS has a built-in `say` command that's free, local, and instant with zero installation. The quality is decent, especially if the user has downloaded the premium Siri voices. I could use that as the baseline, then layer in something like Kokoro via transformers.js as a higher-quality option.

The right approach is probably a voice provider abstraction in the shared code, similar to how the runner handles CLI providers. That way I can support multiple backends—Kokoro for local synthesis, system commands for TTS and STT, with graceful degradation. But first I need to check what's already in the dependencies and whether the app has any existing speech or voice infrastructure.

All the packages I need are available. The main concern is bundling `@huggingface/transformers` into an Electron renderer with Vite—it's technically possible since kokoro-js does it, but I need to think through the bundle size implications and whether tests will actually run.

Before diving into code, I should nail down the architecture. Voice mode should be a full-screen takeover over the thread, not a side panel—centered orb with cards appearing underneath as the agent generates them, matching ChatGPT's approach. The key difference from GPT-Live is that Crew's cards should reflect what the agent actually did: tool steps, diffs, files, boards, task lists, and other native Crew artifacts rather than generic chat cards.

I'm thinking the agent should be able to emit its own card format through a small vocabulary in its reply—lists, key-value facts, choice buttons, images, code—that Crew renders as cards while excluding the markup from the spoken text. That's genuine generative UI that stays true to the app's design.

For the conversation itself, I need to decide whether voice runs in a ghost thread private to the window or in an ordinary thread that the crew can see. The honest choice is a normal thread so the agent's work and the user's request are both visible to the crew. So the conversation becomes a real thread that the whole crew can see and reference. That's simpler to build and way more useful than hiding it away.

The pipeline flows from the microphone through voice activity detection and transcription, then sends the text as a message into the thread where the agent picks it up and runs. The agent's response gets converted back to speech through a text-to-speech model, plays through the web audio system, and the sound visualization responds to what's playing. If I start speaking while the agent is talking, the system detects the new speech and cancels the playback and current run so I can interrupt.

For true full-duplex conversation like GPT-Live does, I'd keep the microphone open during playback and use echo cancellation so the agent's own voice doesn't get picked up by the mic. That's what makes barge-in work without needing headphones.

Now I'm wondering about streaming the TTS output — the text-to-speech library has streaming capabilities, but the agent gives me the full response text all at once along with intermediate steps. I need to check whether the agent actually streams the assistant's text as it generates it or if I'm getting it all at the end.

For the providers, I'm looking at free and local options: Whisper for speech-to-recognition via transformers.js with WebGPU support where available, Kokoro for TTS, and Silero for voice activity detection since it's much more reliable than a simple energy-based VAD — no false positives on keyboard clicks. The VAD library needs a worklet and model files served, which gets tricky in Electron since it defaults to fetching from a CDN.

Actually, given Crew's philosophy of building primitives ourselves rather than pulling in dependencies, I should write a custom VAD in the media module based on the existing speaking monitor pattern. An energy-based approach with adaptive noise floor and zero-crossing detection works well for a desktop app with echo cancellation, keeps dependencies minimal, and aligns with the project's ethos. I'll model it after the speaking monitor but tune it for utterance endpoints with a pre-roll buffer, which leaves just `kokoro-js` and `@huggingface/transformers` as external dependencies.

Since `kokoro-js` already depends on `@huggingface/transformers`, I really just need that one library for both Whisper and TTS. The challenge is model downloads — Whisper base is around 50MB and Kokoro another 86MB, so first run will be slow. I need to show a loading state with a progress indicator on the orb while models cache in the browser. And since these models load in the renderer, I should move them to a Web Worker to keep the UI responsive — that's standard practice with transformers.js, so I'll set up dedicated workers for speech-to-text and text-to-speech.

For the orb itself, I'm thinking it should be the mark's mesh pattern breathing and pulsing with the voice, using the color palette from `MESH_COLORS` that's already established in the app. Drawing the canvas visualization... Defining card types...

The agent outputs fenced card blocks in JSON that `readCards` extracts, leaving just the spoken text behind. Choice options feed back as the next turn. I'll also surface the automatic cards—file changes, diffs, commands—as a small stack near the orb during voice playback.

I need to scope this carefully. The card deck shows what the agent wrote plus its current live step, reusing existing components where possible. Looking at the file structure: `voice.ts` handles the card schema and system preamble, while the media layer manages VAD, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and the state machine that cycles through idle, listening, thinking, and speaking.

So the plan is to build a toast state module with a comprehensive API supporting success/error/info variants, loading states with resolution, deduplication by key, and promise handling, then render a Toaster component in the App, and wire the ephemeral server notices to use toasts instead of chat messages via a new `notice` protocol message that the renderer converts to a toast notification.

step.text:
I'm organizing the implementation into concrete tasks, starting with a shared vocabulary module that defines the voice card structure, a function to parse spoken text into cards, and a system prompt that instructs the agent how to respond concisely to voice input and format card output.

For the audio pipeline, I need to strip markdown before speaking (removing code blocks, links, bullets, and headings), then build out the voice activity detection as a pure testable class that reads audio levels to distinguish speech from silence. The workers handle the heavy lifting—one for transcription via Whisper and another for text-to-speech via Kokoro—while separate modules manage the microphone capture chain (resampling to 16kHz and buffering utterances) and speaker output (queuing PCM data and routing through WebAudio). The session state machine ties everything together, and then I'm building the visual layer with an animated orb component, screen layouts for displaying captions and cards, and finally wiring it all into the UI.

For audio resampling, the mic captures at the system rate (48kHz) but Whisper expects 16kHz mono Float32 data. I'll use an AudioWorklet to pull raw frames—it's the modern approach compared to the deprecated ScriptProcessor. Rather than wrestling with build config, I can embed the worklet as a string and register it via a blob URL, which is a solid pattern that avoids extra file dependencies.

Actually, I'm second-guessing the approach. Using an AnalyserNode with periodic polling loses samples between reads, so it won't capture the full utterance faithfully. I need every sample. MediaRecorder is another option—record to webm/opus, then decode the blob with `decodeAudioData`—but that adds latency on start/stop and doesn't handle pre-roll well.

AudioWorklet is the right choice here. I'll set it up to post Float32Array frames (batched to around 1024 samples) to the main thread, then downsample from 48k to 16k, maintain a rolling pre-roll buffer, run VAD on RMS, and hand off the utterance when the endpoint is detected.

Before I start building, let me check what's already in the codebase—specifically whether `capture.ts` already has a mic stream hooked up, and what the audio and device modules look like.

I've confirmed that TestUi properly tracks all messages and can wait for ServerMessage assertions, so notices are testable. Now I'm designing the toast API and starting to define the core types—setting up the tone variants and action interface for the toast system.

Refining the naming: following the writing rules from AGENTS.md where headings stand alone and secondary text only appears when necessary, a toast should be one line with an optional second line. I'm renaming `text` to be the main line and `detail` for that rare secondary information, so `toast('Copied')` passes a simple string while options can include `detail?`.

For the API shape, I'm using `Object.assign` to make `toast` both a callable function and an object with methods like `done`, `fail`, `busy`, `close`, and `clear` — this matches the industry standard from libraries like sonner and reads naturally as `toast.fail('...')`. The core function takes a text string and optional settings, returning a handle with an id and methods to update or close the toast.

For the toast behavior, I'm setting default durations where `busy` stays indefinitely with a spinner, while success and regular toasts default to 4 seconds and failures to 6 seconds. I'm also adding deduplication by key so that repeated toasts with the same key rewrite in place rather than stacking, and when identical text arrives while a toast is still visible, I'll show a repeat count badge instead of creating duplicates — this is a nice touch for an app like Crew that might generate the same error multiple times.

For notice toasts specifically, I'm using a composite key like `'notice:' + text` so that identical notices collapse into one while different notice messages still stack, preventing the loss of distinct information. I'll also add a timer pause when hovering over the toast stack so users can read without it disappearing.

For the implementation, I'm storing timers in the state module alongside the toast list, using a single interval to manage all timeouts. For status indicators, positive and danger colors are appropriate since the mark represents status, which is an exception to the general rule. The action button is a small pill with a subtle background and hover state, and I'm considering whether the close icon should always be visible or appear only on hover like in Sonner.

On a floating glass card, a persistent close button adds visual clutter, so showing it on hover of the stack makes sense. I can use a CSS keyframe animation on grid-template-rows itself — modern browsers support animating that property, so I can go from 0fr to 1fr in the keyframes. + // A voice thread is an ordinary thread somebody is talking to out loud. What
+ // the agent writes back is read by a voice on the asker's machine, so it is
+ // said in spoken words, and anything worth looking at rather than hearing is
+ // drawn as a card instead of described.
+ 
+ export interface VoiceFact {
+   label: string
+   value: string
+ }
+ 
+ export type VoiceCard =
+   | { kind: 'facts'; title?: string; rows: VoiceFact[] }
+   | { kind: 'list'; title?: string; items: string[] }
+   | { kind: 'choice'; title?: string; options: string[] }
+   | { kind: 'code'; title?: string; language?: string; text: string }
+   | { kind: 'note'; title?: string; text: string }
+ 
+ export type VoiceCardKind = VoiceCard['kind']
+ 
+ export const TITLE_LIMIT = 48
+ export const LABEL_LIMIT = 32
+ export const VALUE_LIMIT = 64
+ export const ITEM_LIMIT = 120
+ export const OPTION_LIMIT = 40
+ export const TEXT_LIMIT = 800
+ export const ROWS_LIMIT = 8
+ export const ITEMS_LIMIT = 8
+ export const OPTIONS_LIMIT = 4
+ export const CARDS_LIMIT = 3
+ export const LANGUAGE_LIMIT = 16
+ 
+ const line = (value: unknown, limit: number): string =>
+   typeof value === 'string' ? value.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim().slice(0, limit) : ''
+ 
+ const block = (value: unknown, limit: number): string =>
+   typeof value === 'string' ? value.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n').trim().slice(0, limit) : ''
+ 
+ const titled = <T extends object>(card: T, title: string): T => (title ? { ...card, title } : card)
+ 
+ const strings = (value: unknown, limit: number, count: number): string[] =>
+   Array.isArray(value)
+     ? value
+         .map(item => line(item, limit))
+         .filter(Boolean)
+         .slice(0, count)
+     : []
+ 
+ // What arrives is whatever a model wrote, so a card is only as good as this. One
+ // with nothing on it is not a card and comes back as null rather than as an
+ // empty box standing beside the orb.
+ export function cleanCard(raw: unknown): VoiceCard | null {
+   if (!raw || typeof raw !== 'object') return null
+   const card = raw as Record<string, unknown>
+   const title = line(card.title, TITLE_LIMIT)
+   if (card.kind === 'facts') {
+     const rows = Array.isArray(card.rows)
+       ? card.rows
+           .map(row => {
+             const entry = (row ?? {}) as Record<string, unknown>
+             return { label: line(entry.label, LABEL_LIMIT), value: line(entry.value, VALUE_LIMIT) }
+           })
+           .filter(row => row.label !== '' || row.value !== '')
+           .slice(0, ROWS_LIMIT)
+       : []
+     return rows.length > 0 ? titled({ kind: 'facts' as const, rows }, title) : null
+   }
+   if (card.kind === 'list') {
+     const items = strings(card.items, ITEM_LIMIT, ITEMS_LIMIT)
+     return items.length > 0 ? titled({ kind: 'list' as const, items }, title) : null
+   }
+   if (card.kind === 'choice') {
+     const options = strings(card.options, OPTION_LIMIT, OPTIONS_LIMIT)
+     return options.length > 0 ? titled({ kind: 'choice' as const, options }, title) : null
+   }
+   if (card.kind === 'code') {
+     const text = block(card.text, TEXT_LIMIT)
+     if (!text) return null
+     const language = line(card.language, LANGUAGE_LIMIT).toLowerCase()
+     return titled(language ? { kind: 'code' as const, language, text } : { kind: 'code' as const, text }, title)
+   }
+   if (card.kind === 'note') {
+     const text = block(card.text, TEXT_LIMIT)
+     return text ? titled({ kind: 'note' as const, text }, title) : null
+   }
+   return null
+ }
+ 
+ const CARD_FENCE = /^[ \t]*```[ \t]*card[ \t]*\r?\n([\s\S]*?)^[ \t]*```[ \t]*$/gim
+ 
+ // A card is a fenced block the agent writes beside its words. It is taken out
+ // of what gets said, because the whole point of one is that it is looked at.
+ export function readCards(text: string): { spoken: string; cards: VoiceCard[] } {
+   const cards: VoiceCard[] = []
+   const spoken = text.replace(CARD_FENCE, (whole, body: string) => {
+     if (cards.length >= CARDS_LIMIT) return ''
+     try {
+       const card = cleanCard(JSON.parse(body))
+       if (card) cards.push(card)
+     } catch {
+       return ''
+     }
+     return ''
+   })
+   return { spoken, cards }
+ }
+ 
+ const EMOJI = /[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\u{1f3fb}-\u{1f3ff}‍️]/gu
+ 
+ // Everything a page can show and a voice cannot say. Read straight, a reply
+ // comes out as "star star ready star star", and one stray backtick is enough to
+ // make the whole answer sound like it is being spelled out.
+ export function spokenText(text: string): string {
+   return text
+     .replace(/\r\n/g, '\n')
+     .replace(/^[ \t]*```[\s\S]*?^[ \t]*```[ \t]*$/gim, '')
+     .replace(/`([^`\n]+)`/g, '$1')
+     .replace(/!\[[^\]]*\]\([^)]*\)/g, '')
+     .replace(/\[([^\]]+)\]\([^)]*\)/g, '$1')
+     .replace(/<https?:\/\/[^>\s]+>/g, '')
+     .replace(/https?:\/\/\S+/g, '')
+     .replace(/^[ \t]*#{1,6}[ \t]+/gm, '')
+     .replace(/^[ \t]*>[ \t]?/gm, '')
+     .replace(/^[ \t]*([-*_])(?:[ \t]*\1){2,}[ \t]*$/gm, '')
+     .replace(/^[ \t]*\|.*\|[ \t]*$/gm, row => row.replace(/\|/g, ' ').trim())
+     .replace(/^[ \t]*[-*+][ \t]+/gm, '')
+     .replace(/\*\*([^*]+)\*\*/g, '$1')
+     .replace(/(^|[\s(])\*([^*\n]+)\*(?=[\s).,!?;:]|$)/g, '$1$2')
+     .replace(/(^|[\s(])_([^_\n]+)_(?=[\s).,!?;:]|$)/g, '$1$2')
+     .replace(/(^|\s)@([\w-]+)/g, '$1$2')
+     .replace(EMOJI, '')
+     .replace(/[ \t]+/g, ' ')
+     .replace(/[ \t]+$/gm, '')
+     .replace(/\n{3,}/g, '\n\n')
+     .trim()
+ }
+ 
+ // Both halves of a reply in one pass: the words to say, and what to draw.
+ export function readReply(text: string): { spoken: string; cards: VoiceCard[] } {
+   const { spoken, cards } = readCards(text)
+   return { spoken: spokenText(spoken), cards }
+ }
+ 
+ export const VOICE_INSTRUCTIONS = [
+   'This thread is a voice conversation. Every message here was spoken out loud, and your reply is read back by a voice, so write it the way you would say it.',
+   'Answer in a sentence or two. Plain spoken words, no markdown, no headings, no bullet lists, no code, no emoji, and never read a file path or a URL out loud.',
+   'Do the work you are asked to do as usual. When you have done something, say what you did in one line rather than listing it.',
+   'When there is something worth looking at rather than hearing, put it on a card and keep saying your one line beside it. A card is a fenced block written exactly like this:',
+   '```card',
+   '{"kind":"facts","title":"Suite","rows":[{"label":"Passed","value":"84"},{"label":"Failed","value":"2"}]}',
+   '```',
+   `The kinds are facts with rows of label and value, list with items, choice with up to ${OPTIONS_LIMIT} options for someone to pick from out loud, code with text and an optional language, and note with text.`,
+   `Write at most ${CARDS_LIMIT} cards, only when they earn their place, and never a card that just repeats what you said.`
+ ].join('\n')
+

Now I'm ready to write out the implementation files: the toast state management, the Toaster component, the CSS styling, mounting it in the app, and handling the protocol notice, server session notice, and store interactions.

I'm defining the toast state module with types for different toast tones, actions, and options, then setting up the internal state management with a limit of 4 concurrent toasts, an exit animation duration of 180ms, and timing rules for how long each tone should display.

Defining the core functions to manage toast lifecycle... Adding more handler logic... I'm reconsidering the handle design — instead of exposing `id` on the handle itself, I'll track the current live id internally and have all handle methods reference that, keeping the interface simpler. Then I'm setting up `useToasts()` as a hook that subscribes to external store changes and returns the current toasts array.

For the Toast component, I need to handle the `mark` prop with sensible defaults based on tone — checkmark for success, warning icon for errors, spinner for loading states, and nothing for plain messages. Now I'm importing the necessary dependencies and setting up the component structure.

I'm debating whether to import `TOP_BAR_H` from TopBar or define it locally to avoid pulling in heavy dependencies like the store and audio system during tests. The toaster needs to know the top bar height for positioning, but I could use a CSS variable instead to keep the modules decoupled.

For closing toasts, I'll export a `closeToast(id)` function that the Row component can call when the user clicks close, separate from the public `toast.*` API. I'll also add `toast.clear()` for clearing all toasts at once.

Building the Row component... Finishing the close button with the icon, then reconsidering the text wrapping approach. Since toasts can have longer messages, I should allow wrapping instead of truncating, using `text-pretty` for better line breaks. The mark alignment needs to adjust too—using `items-start` when text wraps across multiple lines, similar to how AGENTS.md handles faces beside paragraphs.

For the close button, I'll keep it in the layout at all times but fade its opacity on hover using a `group` wrapper. The toast container itself should be 320px wide, positioned at `right-6` to match the top bar spacing, and I'm setting up the portal structure with `aria-live="polite"` for accessibility.

I need to use `z-[45]` since that's not a standard Tailwind value. The `pointer-events-none` on the container prevents the invisible space around the toasts from blocking clicks on the app behind it — since the container shrinks to fit its content width with `flex flex-col` and fixed positioning, there could still be dead zones that interfere with interaction.

I'm setting `pointer-events-auto` on each card so they remain interactive, and React's synthetic `onPointerEnter` will still fire on the container when the pointer enters a child element because React simulates enter/leave semantics from the underlying `pointerover`/`pointerout` events, which do propagate through the element tree even though native pointer enter/leave events don't bubble.

Let me check where `TOP_BAR_H` is imported and used—it's not rendered in `Home`, so the toast positioned at top 70 should be fine. The top bar container is at `z-40`, so I need to make sure the z-index stacking is correct.

All 20 tests passed on the first run, so task 1 is complete. Moving on to task 2 now—building the ear component. I'm planning three files: a pure VAD module with testable numbers, the main ear file that chains together the microphone, audio worklet, resampling, and gate logic to produce utterances, and a worker for Whisper integration. Let me focus on the gate implementation first and think through how it should work.

The voice gate needs to track an adaptive noise floor from incoming RMS levels and decide when speech starts and stops. I'm designing it as a simple state machine that returns 'idle', 'speaking', or 'ended' on each frame push. The adaptive floor uses fast decay when levels drop below it and slow rise when they're above it, creating natural hysteresis. Speech opens when the level exceeds the floor by a multiplier plus margin, and closes after sustained silence. I'm also adding constraints for minimum utterance length to filter out clicks and coughs, plus a maximum length cap.

The app already has absolute thresholds like `START_LEVEL = 0.028` that serve as a safety floor so silence never triggers the gate. I'll layer the adaptive floor above that baseline. Since frames arrive at 32ms intervals from 512-sample hops at 16kHz, that gives good temporal resolution.

For barge-in protection when the agent is speaking, I'm exposing a `guarded()` method that raises the open threshold and extends the opening delay, avoiding false triggers from echo. Now I'm moving to implement the gate class itself, then the ear module which handles downsampling audio from 48kHz to 16kHz, buffering pre-roll to capture word onsets, and concatenating the full utterance when speech ends.

Writing gate.ts... Writing the resampler and worker setup... Both quantized model variants are correctly mapped across the repos—`q8` suffixes align with the quantized file naming. Now I'm setting up the audio processing pipeline with separate modules for the voice activity detection gate and resampling logic.

Defining the gate constants and interface... Writing gate logic... I should return `'dropped'` instead of `'quiet'` to make it explicit when an utterance is abandoned, so the caller knows to clear the buffer. I'm also thinking about adding a `reset()` method for when listening stops, and I need to expose the audio level to the orb so it can react to the user's voice — the ear already computes this, so I can expose a smoothed `level` value that the orb can read directly.

For richer orb modulation, I want frequency bands rather than just RMS. I'll attach an AnalyserNode to both the mouth's output (for the agent's voice) and the mic source (for the user's voice), giving me 5 bands in both directions without extra FFT work.

I'm creating a small helper in `voiceLevels.ts` that extracts N bands plus overall RMS from an AnalyserNode — something both ear and mouth can use. Let me check how `Bars.tsx` handles the banding convention so I can stay consistent.

Now I need to run the full test suite for the related modules I modified—browser-tabs-probe, side-panel-resize-probe, plan-card-probe, plan.integration, and browser-image-probe—along with a typecheck to verify the CrewBridge type is properly recognized across the test files.
Now the ear. Starting with the pure pieces so they're testable on their own:

I'm setting up a state management module using React's external store hook, and I want to support toast notifications that can display an agent's icon or avatar through a `mark` prop, plus an `action` field for things like jumping to a thread.

Writing the state module... Writing the toast module... Writing timer management functions... Finishing the toast control logic...

I'm thinking through the test cleanup issue — `clearToasts()` animates the removal which leaves a 180ms window, making tests flaky with real timers. I could add a `now` parameter for immediate clearing, or use a test-only reset function, but that feels messy. Better approach: tests can just call `clearToasts()` and advance the fake timers, or rely on component cleanup between cases since the toast state is module-level anyway.

For the `show` function, I'm building the core logic that takes a text string and optional configuration, determines the tone and duration, checks if there's an existing toast with the same key that's still visible, and generates a unique ID.  If a matching toast exists, I update it in place; otherwise I add the new toast to the stack and trim any excess beyond the limit. Then I set up the auto-dismiss timer and return a handle for controlling it.

For the `handle` function, I'm creating a closure that tracks the toast's ID and closed state, providing methods to check if it's still alive and to update its text. Completing the handle object with methods for updating the toast text, marking it as done or failed with appropriate tones, and closing it, while also tracking whether the toast is still alive to decide between rewriting an existing toast or creating a new one. ...toasts]), then filtering out any old toasts beyond the limit and re-arming the timer for the new one. The `rewrite` function updates an existing toast by recording the new text and options, editing it in place, and re-arming its timer. Then I'm exporting a `toast` function using Object.assign that wraps the `raise` logic, along with convenience methods for different toast types like `done`, `fail`, and `busy`.

Now I'm refactoring this to be more DRY by extracting the tone-specific logic into a helper function that returns a configured handler, so each tone variant just calls the same underlying `open` function with the appropriate tone set. Then I'm moving on to the `useToasts` hook that syncs with the external store...

Finishing the hook implementation with a listener function that manages subscriptions, and the TypeScript void return type works fine even though `delete` returns a boolean. Now I'm building the `Toaster` component that renders the toast rows, where each row displays a different icon or spinner based on the toast's tone—checkmark for done, warning for fail, spinner for busy, and nothing for plain. Writing component markup... I should change the aria-label to "Close" to match the app's voice better. The Toaster component itself creates a fixed positioned container that holds all the toast notifications, positioned near the top right of the screen with pointer event handlers to pause and resume the toast queue.

For accessibility, I'm deciding between putting aria-live on the container versus individual toast rows — having both can cause double announcements, so I'll put role="status" or role="alert" on each toast card instead, letting screen readers announce them as they're inserted into the DOM.

I should also return null when there are no toasts to avoid rendering an empty fixed div, even though pointer-events-none makes it harmless. On positioning, the toast's right edge should align with the TopBar's right padding and the profile avatar, and I need to add some vertical spacing between the toast and the header bottom rather than having it flush against it. I'll go with the container having `pt-2` and each card slot getting `pb-2` for consistent spacing. Now I'm writing the CSS to style the toast notification container that slides in from the right under the header. Still writing animation styles...

I need to add the reduced motion rule for the toast row animations, then figure out where to place these styles in the existing stylesheet. After that, I'm updating the protocol to include a notice message type in the ServerMessage union.

Now I'm wiring up the notice functionality by adding a method to send these ephemeral messages to clients, then replacing three specific ghost and plan command messages with calls to this new notice method — I need to make sure the WebSocket is available in scope at those call sites.

For the store, I'm handling the notice message type by showing it as a plain toast without any warning styling, since these are informational responses rather than errors. Then I want to use this same pattern in the renderer, specifically when the invite fails in TopBar — if the share operation doesn't return a link, I'll show a plain-language notice about the session not being shareable, so I need to check what the share function does on failure first.

+ // Where one thing somebody said starts and where it ends. A level alone cannot
+ // answer that: a room has a floor of its own, a sentence has gaps in it, and a
+ // chair moving is louder than a word. The gate watches the floor the room is
+ // sitting at and opens on whatever stands well above it for long enough.
+ 
+ export const HEARD_RATE = 16000
+ 
+ // 32ms of sound at the rate whisper listens at. Fine enough to catch the front
+ // of a word and coarse enough that a click is one frame and never two.
+ export const FRAME = 512
+ 
+ export type GateWord = 'quiet' | 'speaking' | 'ended' | 'dropped'
+ 
+ // Nothing under this is ever speech, however quiet the room gets. Without it a
+ // silent room walks its own floor down to nothing and starts hearing the fans.
+ const NEVER_UNDER = 0.0018
+ const ALWAYS_OVER = 0.0125
+ 
+ const OPEN_OVER = 2.6
+ const CLOSE_OVER = 1.5
+ 
+ // The floor drops to a quiet room quickly and climbs to a loud one slowly, so
+ // somebody talking steadily never raises the floor past their own voice.
+ const FALL = 0.35
+ const RISE = 0.004
+ 
+ const OPEN_MS = 96
+ const CLOSE_MS = 620
+ const SHORTEST_MS = 240
+ const LONGEST_MS = 30_000
+ 
+ // Echo cancellation leaves some of the agent's own voice in the microphone, so
+ // while it is talking the gate asks for more before it believes it is being
+ // interrupted. Loose here and the agent talks itself到 a stop.
+ const GUARD_OVER = 2.2
+ const GUARD_MS = 220
+ 
+ export class VoiceGate {
+   private floor = ALWAYS_OVER
+   private open = false
+   private loudMs = 0
+   private quietMs = 0
+   private heldMs = 0
+   private guard = false
+ 
+   // On while the agent is speaking, which is the only time the microphone is
+   // hearing something the room did not make.
+   guarded(on: boolean): void {
+     this.guard = on
+   }
+ 
+   get speaking(): boolean {
+     return this.open
+   }
+ 
+   get noiseFloor(): number {
+     return this.floor
+   }
+ 
+   reset(): void {
+     this.open = false
+     this.loudMs = 0
+     this.quietMs = 0
+     this.heldMs = 0
+   }
+ 
+   push(level: number, ms: number): GateWord {
+     const opensAt = Math.max(ALWAYS_OVER, this.floor * OPEN_OVER) * (this.guard ? GUARD_OVER : 1)
+     const closesAt = Math.max(ALWAYS_OVER * 0.55, this.floor * CLOSE_OVER)
+     if (!this.open) {
+       // The floor only moves while nobody is talking. Tracked through an
+       // utterance it climbs into the voice and closes the gate mid-sentence.
+       this.floor = Math.max(NEVER_UNDER, this.floor + (level - this.floor) * (level < this.floor ? FALL : RISE))
+       this.loudMs = level > opensAt ? this.loudMs + ms : 0
+       if (this.loudMs < (this.guard ? GUARD_MS : OPEN_MS)) return 'quiet'
+       this.open = true
+       this.heldMs = this.loudMs
+       this.quietMs = 0
+       return 'speaking'
+     }
+     this.heldMs += ms
+     this.quietMs = level < closesAt ? this.quietMs + ms : 0
+     if (this.quietMs >= CLOSE_MS || this.heldMs >= LONGEST_MS) return this.close()
+     return 'speaking'
+   }
+ 
+   // A cough, a door, one syllable of nothing. Long enough to open the gate and
+   // too short to be worth sending anywhere.
+   private close(): GateWord {
+     const said = this.heldMs - this.quietMs >= SHORTEST_MS
+     this.reset()
+     return said ? 'ended' : 'dropped'
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ export const rmsOf = (frame: Float32Array): number => {
+   let sum = 0
+   for (const sample of frame) sum += sample * sample
+   return Math.sqrt(sum / Math.max(1, frame.length))
+ }

+ import { useSyncExternalStore, type ReactNode } from 'react'
+ 
+ // A word from the app about what just happened, standing under the header for a
+ // few seconds. Nothing anybody has to come back to is ever said here: that goes
+ // in the chat, in a thread, or on the row it is about.
+ export type ToastTone = 'plain' | 'done' | 'fail' | 'busy'
+ 
+ export interface ToastAction {
+   label: string
+   onPress: () => void
+   // The row goes when the button is pressed, unless the press is the start of
+   // something rather than the end of it.
+   keep?: boolean
+ }
+ 
+ export interface ToastOptions {
+   tone?: ToastTone
+   detail?: string
+   mark?: ReactNode
+   action?: ToastAction
+   seconds?: number
+   // One row per key. Asked for again under the same key, the row standing is
+   // rewritten where it stands rather than a second one arriving under it.
+   key?: string
+ }
+ 
+ export interface Toast extends ToastOptions {
+   id: string
+   text: string
+   tone: ToastTone
+   seconds: number
+   leaving?: boolean
+ }
+ 
+ export interface ToastHandle {
+   set: (text: string, opts?: ToastOptions) => void
+   done: (text: string, opts?: ToastOptions) => void
+   fail: (text: string, opts?: ToastOptions) => void
+   close: () => void
+ }
+ 
+ const STAY: Record<ToastTone, number> = { plain: 4, done: 4, fail: 8, busy: 0 }
+ const LIMIT = 4
+ 
+ export const TOAST_OUT_MS = 180
+ 
+ interface Clock {
+   left: number
+   at: number
+   timer?: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>
+ }
+ 
+ let toasts: Toast[] = []
+ let held = false
+ let made = 0
+ const listeners = new Set<() => void>()
+ const clocks = new Map<string, Clock>()
+ 
+ function tell(): void {
+   for (const listener of listeners) listener()
+ }
+ 
+ function put(next: Toast[]): void {
+   toasts = next
+   tell()
+ }
+ 
+ function start(id: string): void {
+   const clock = clocks.get(id)
+   if (!clock || clock.timer || held) return
+   clock.at = Date.now()
+   clock.timer = setTimeout(() => closeToast(id), clock.left)
+ }
+ 
+ function pause(id: string): void {
+   const clock = clocks.get(id)
+   if (!clock?.timer) return
+   clearTimeout(clock.timer)
+   clock.timer = undefined
+   clock.left = Math.max(0, clock.left - (Date.now() - clock.at))
+ }
+ 
+ function arm(id: string, seconds: number): void {
+   const clock = clocks.get(id)
+   if (clock?.timer) clearTimeout(clock.timer)
+   clocks.delete(id)
+   if (seconds <= 0) return
+   clocks.set(id, { left: seconds * 1000, at: Date.now() })
+   start(id)
+ }
+ 
+ function record(id: string, text: string, opts: ToastOptions): Toast {
+   const tone = opts.tone ?? 'plain'
+   return { ...opts, id, text, tone, seconds: opts.seconds ?? STAY[tone] }
+ }
+ 
+ function rewrite(id: string, text: string, opts: ToastOptions): string {
+   const next = record(id, text, opts)
+   put(toasts.map(t => (t.id === id ? next : t)))
+   arm(id, next.seconds)
+   return id
+ }
+ 
+ function raise(text: string, opts: ToastOptions): string {
+   const standing = opts.key ? toasts.find(t => t.key === opts.key && !t.leaving) : undefined
+   if (standing) return rewrite(standing.id, text, opts)
+   const next = record(`toast:${++made}`, text, opts)
+   put([next, ...toasts])
+   for (const old of toasts.filter(t => !t.leaving).slice(LIMIT)) closeToast(old.id)
+   arm(next.id, next.seconds)
+   return next.id
+ }
+ 
+ // A row leaves in two beats: it is marked on the way out so the stack can close
+ // over it, and it is really gone once that has played.
+ export function closeToast(id: string): void {
+   const going = toasts.find(t => t.id === id)
+   if (!going || going.leaving) return
+   const clock = clocks.get(id)
+   if (clock?.timer) clearTimeout(clock.timer)
+   clocks.delete(id)
+   put(toasts.map(t => (t.id === id ? { ...t, leaving: true } : t)))
+   setTimeout(() => put(toasts.filter(t => t.id !== id)), TOAST_OUT_MS)
+ }
+ 
+ export function clearToasts(): void {
+   for (const t of toasts) closeToast(t.id)
+ }
+ 
+ // Nothing runs out while it is being read. The pointer resting anywhere on the
+ // stack holds every clock in it, and lifting it hands back what was left.
+ export function holdToasts(on: boolean): void {
+   if (held === on) return
+   held = on
+   for (const id of [...clocks.keys()]) (on ? pause : start)(id)
+ }
+ 
+ function handle(first: string): ToastHandle {
+   let id = first
+   let closed = false
+   const live = (): boolean => toasts.some(t => t.id === id && !t.leaving)
+   // A run that was going long enough for its row to have gone still has
+   // something to say at the end of it, so it says it as a row of its own.
+   const again = (text: string, opts: ToastOptions): void => {
+     if (closed) return
+     id = live() ? rewrite(id, text, opts) : raise(text, opts)
+   }
+   return {
+     set: (text, opts = {}) => {
+       if (!closed && live()) rewrite(id, text, opts)
+     },
+     done: (text, opts = {}) => again(text, { ...opts, tone: opts.tone ?? 'done' }),
+     fail: (text, opts = {}) => again(text, { ...opts, tone: opts.tone ?? 'fail' }),
+     close: () => {
+       closed = true
+       closeToast(id)
+     }
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ function open(text: string, opts: ToastOptions = {}): ToastHandle {
+   return handle(raise(text, opts))
+ }
+ 
+ function inTone(tone: ToastTone) {
+   return (text: string, opts: ToastOptions = {}): ToastHandle => open(text, { ...opts, tone })
+ }
+ 
+ export const toast = Object.assign(open, {
+   done: inTone('done'),
+   fail: inTone('fail'),
+   busy: inTone('busy')
+ })
+ 
+ export function useToasts(): Toast[] {
+   return useSyncExternalStore(listener => {
+     listeners.add(listener)
+     return () => listeners.delete(listener)
+   }, () => toasts)
+ }
+

+ import type { MediaKind } from '../../../../shared/media'
+ import { context } from '../audio'
+ import { captureMic } from '../capture'
+ import { storedInput } from '../devices'
+ import { EAR_PROCESSOR, EAR_SOURCE } from './earWorklet'
+ import { FRAME, HEARD_RATE, rmsOf, VoiceGate } from './gate'
+ import { join, PreRoll, resample } from './resample'
+ 
+ const PRE_ROLL_MS = 320
+ 
+ export interface EarEars {
+   // The moment the gate opens, which is also the moment somebody has cut in on
+   // the agent. It arrives before the words do, because stopping the voice is
+   // the one thing that cannot wait for whisper.
+   onStart: () => void
+   onEnd: (audio: Float32Array, seconds: number) => void
+ }
+ 
+ const loaded = new WeakSet<AudioContext>()
+ 
+ async function loadWorklet(ctx: AudioContext): Promise<boolean> {
+   if (loaded.has(ctx)) return true
+   if (!ctx.audioWorklet) return false
+   const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([EAR_SOURCE], { type: 'application/javascript' }))
+   try {
+     await ctx.audioWorklet.addModule(url)
+     loaded.add(ctx)
+     return true
+   } catch {
+     return false
+   } finally {
+     URL.revokeObjectURL(url)
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ // The microphone, listened to for the start and end of things somebody says.
+ // It stays open for the whole conversation, the agent's turn included, which is
+ // what lets somebody talk over the answer rather than wait it out.
+ export class VoiceEar {
+   private track: MediaStreamTrack | null = null
+   private source: MediaStreamAudioSourceNode | null = null
+   private node: AudioWorkletNode | null = null
+   private sink: GainNode | null = null
+   private gate = new VoiceGate()
+   private preRoll = new PreRoll(Math.round((HEARD_RATE * PRE_ROLL_MS) / 1000))
+   private said: Float32Array[] = []
+   private spare = new Float32Array(0)
+   private off = false
+ 
+   analyser: AnalyserNode | null = null
+ 
+   constructor(private readonly ears: EarEars) {}
+ 
+   async open(): Promise<MediaKind | null> {
+     const ctx = context()
+     if (!ctx) return 'microphone'
+     if (!(await loadWorklet(ctx))) return 'microphone'
+     const { track, problem } = await captureMic(storedInput('microphone'))
+     if (!track) return problem ?? 'microphone'
+     this.track = track
+     this.source = ctx.createMediaStreamSource(new MediaStream([track]))
+     this.analyser = ctx.createAnalyser()
+     this.analyser.fftSize = 1024
+     this.analyser.smoothingTimeConstant = 0.55
+     this.node = new AudioWorkletNode(ctx, EAR_PROCESSOR)
+     this.node.port.onmessage = event => this.hear(event.data as Float32Array, ctx.sampleRate)
+     this.source.connect(this.analyser)
+     this.source.connect(this.node)
+     // A worklet with nowhere to go is not pulled at all in some builds, so it
+     // runs into a gain of nothing rather than into the speakers.
+     this.sink = ctx.createGain()
+     this.sink.gain.value = 0
+     this.node.connect(this.sink)
+     this.sink.connect(ctx.destination)
+     return null
+   }
+ 
+   // Off is the microphone itself off, not a gate held shut, so nothing in the
+   // room reaches the app at all while it is.
+   mute(on: boolean): void {
+     this.off = on
+     if (this.track) this.track.enabled = !on
+     if (!on) return
+     this.gate.reset()
+     this.preRoll.clear()
+     this.said = []
+     this.spare = new Float32Array(0)
+   }
+ 
+   get muted(): boolean {
+     return this.off
+   }
+ 
+   guarded(on: boolean): void {
+     this.gate.guarded(on)
+   }
+ 
+   close(): void {
+     this.node?.port.close()
+     this.node?.disconnect()
+     this.sink?.disconnect()
+     this.analyser?.disconnect()
+     this.source?.disconnect()
+     this.track?.stop()
+     this.node = null
+     this.sink = null
+     this.analyser = null
+     this.source = null
+     this.track = null
+     this.gate.reset()
+     this.preRoll.clear()
+     this.said = []
+   }
+ 
+   private hear(block: Float32Array, rate: number): void {
+     if (this.off) return
+     const at16 = resample(block, rate, HEARD_RATE)
+     const carried = this.spare.length > 0 ? join([this.spare, at16]) : at16
+     const whole = Math.floor(carried.length / FRAME)
+     this.spare = carried.subarray(whole * FRAME).slice()
+     for (let i = 0; i < whole; i++) {
+       this.frame(carried.subarray(i * FRAME, (i + 1) * FRAME))
+     }
+   }
+ 
+   private frame(frame: Float32Array): void {
+     const was = this.gate.speaking
+     const word = this.gate.push(rmsOf(frame), (FRAME / HEARD_RATE) * 1000)
+     if (word === 'quiet') {
+       this.preRoll.push(frame.slice())
+       return
+     }
+     if (!was) {
+       this.said = this.preRoll.take()
+       this.ears.onStart()
+     }
+     this.said.push(frame.slice())
+     if (word === 'speaking') return
+     const audio = join(this.said)
+     this.said = []
+     this.preRoll.clear()
+     if (word === 'ended') this.ears.onEnd(audio, audio.length / HEARD_RATE)
+   }
+ }

Boot waits 1600ms before calling onDone, so any test that synchronously renders App and immediately asserts will hit the boot screen. Three older test suites were never updated when Boot was added, which is the root cause of the failures. The solution is to make `matchMedia` return `matches: true` for prefers-reduced-motion, which causes Boot to land immediately instead of waiting.

I'm torn on whether to fix those three test suites now. plan-card-probe covers the plan card in chat, which I didn't actually touch — it's failing for an unrelated reason. The fix itself is straightforward: mock reduced motion and flush the 360ms timer. But it's scope creep beyond what was asked, and other people are working in this repo who might already be addressing it. I should flag the issue clearly and move on.

Let me run through one final check: my new probe, the browser suites, and TypeScript, plus the plan integration test to make sure the server-side stuff is unaffected. Then I'll do a design review of the tab switching logic — when you're in a thread with a plan and use the toolbox, everything works. When the plan tab is the only tab and you switch to Docs, the side panel hides correctly. The `openUrl` and `openFile` rules don't clash with the plan tab kind. `hidePlan` picks a neighbor tab properly. The `showPlan` effect on mount is safe even if there's no plan tab yet. And `SidePanel` correctly checks that tabs exist before opening.
Now the protocol and the server.

Now I'm setting up the Whisper worker with a shared model configuration file. I'm going with the `onnx-community/whisper-base.en` model quantized to q8—it's a solid balance between accuracy and size at around 50MB, and significantly better than the tiny variant. For device selection, I'll prioritize WebGPU when available and fall back to WASM, though there's a consideration around how the encoder performs on WebGPU with transformers.js v3.

Actually, I'm reconsidering the device strategy. There's a known issue where Whisper on WebGPU can produce garbage output in certain configurations, so I'll default to WASM for correctness—it handles a 3-second utterance in about 1-2 seconds on an M-series Mac, which is acceptable. For Kokoro TTS, I'll use WebGPU since it's well-supported there and TTS latency matters more for perceived responsiveness since it streams. I'll structure the device selection to be decided once with fallback capability, then define the model constants and voice configuration.

step.text: I'm examining the boot code to understand how it gets triggered, then locating the App flag and Boot view components.
I'll look at how the boot is gated before changing anything.

I'm spotting a race condition where `push` messages arrive before the text splitter is initialized. The issue is that `open` starts the async `speak()` function which awaits the model load, but `push` messages can come in during that wait and get dropped since the splitter doesn't exist yet. I need to create the `TextSplitterStream` synchronously right in the `open` handler, before any async operations, so it's ready to receive pushes immediately.

I'm also reconsidering the audio buffer transfer safety. The `piece.audio.data` getter returns a Float32Array, and if it's backed by a larger shared buffer, transferring it could detach more memory than intended. To be safe, I'll copy the audio data into a fresh Float32Array before transferring the buffer.

For the `stop` handler, incrementing `turn` and closing the splitter should work—it causes `speak()` to bail out early while letting the async generator finish draining. Though there seems to be another issue I'm starting to identify...

Actually, I need to rethink the turn numbering. If `stop` increments `turn` while the main thread assigns `turn = message.turn`, the two could diverge and cause stale checks to misfire. Better approach: have `stop` set `turn = -1` (an unowned turn number) instead of incrementing, keeping the main thread as the sole source of turn assignments.

I should also clean up the voice type casting. Rather than using `as never`, I can define a proper type alias to extract the voice parameter type from the TTS function signature, making the code more readable.

+ import { context } from '../audio'
+ import { SPEAK_RATE } from './models'
+ import type { SpeakIn, SpeakOut } from './speak.worker'
+ 
+ // A little air in front of the first chunk, so scheduling it does not land in
+ // the past on a machine that took a moment to hand the audio over.
+ const LEAD = 0.06
+ 
+ export interface MouthEars {
+   onFetching: (file: string, loaded: number, total: number) => void
+   onReady: () => void
+   // The words of the sentence that has just started coming out, which is what
+   // the caption reads. A sentence at a time is the finest the model works at.
+   onSaying: (text: string) => void
+   onQuiet: () => void
+   onFailed: (message: string) => void
+ }
+ 
+ export class VoiceMouth {
+   private worker: Worker | null = null
+   private out: GainNode | null = null
+   private live: AudioBufferSourceNode[] = []
+   private nextAt = 0
+   private turn = 0
+   private waiting = 0
+   private sealed = true
+ 
+   analyser: AnalyserNode | null = null
+ 
+   constructor(private readonly ears: MouthEars) {}
+ 
+   load(): void {
+     this.hire()?.postMessage({ type: 'load' } satisfies SpeakIn)
+   }
+ 
+   get speaking(): boolean {
+     return this.waiting > 0 || !this.sealed
+   }
+ 
+   // A turn is opened before there is anything to say, so the first sentence the
+   // agent writes is already on its way to the model as it lands.
+   open(voice: string): void {
+     this.silence()
+     this.turn++
+     this.sealed = false
+     this.hire()?.postMessage({ type: 'open', turn: this.turn, voice } satisfies SpeakIn)
+   }
+ 
+   push(text: string): void {
+     if (this.sealed || !text) return
+     this.worker?.postMessage({ type: 'push', turn: this.turn, text } satisfies SpeakIn)
+   }
+ 
+   seal(): void {
+     if (this.sealed) return
+     this.sealed = true
+     this.worker?.postMessage({ type: 'close', turn: this.turn } satisfies SpeakIn)
+     this.settle()
+   }
+ 
+   // Cut in. Everything scheduled goes, and so does everything the model has not
+   // handed over yet, because the one thing an interruption must not do is let
+   // the rest of the old sentence out afterwards.
+   stop(): void {
+     const was = this.speaking
+     this.sealed = true
+     this.turn++
+     this.worker?.postMessage({ type: 'stop' } satisfies SpeakIn)
+     this.silence()
+     if (was) this.ears.onQuiet()
+   }
+ 
+   close(): void {
+     this.silence()
+     this.worker?.terminate()
+     this.worker = null
+     this.out?.disconnect()
+     this.analyser?.disconnect()
+     this.out = null
+     this.analyser = null
+   }
+ 
+   private silence(): void {
+     for (const source of this.live) {
+       source.onended = null
+       try {
+         source.stop()
+       } catch {
+         // Already finished on its own, which is the same silence.
+       }
+       source.disconnect()
+     }
+     this.live = []
+     this.waiting = 0
+     this.nextAt = 0
+   }
+ 
+   private hire(): Worker | null {
+     if (this.worker) return this.worker
+     if (typeof Worker === 'undefined') return null
+     const worker = new Worker(new URL('./speak.worker.ts', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })
+     worker.onmessage = (event: MessageEvent<SpeakOut>) => this.heard(event.data)
+     this.worker = worker
+     return worker
+   }
+ 
+   private heard(message: SpeakOut): void {
+     if (message.type === 'fetching') return this.ears.onFetching(message.file, message.loaded, message.total)
+     if (message.type === 'ready') return this.ears.onReady()
+     if (message.type === 'failed') return this.ears.onFailed(message.message)
+     if (message.turn !== this.turn) return
+     if (message.type === 'done') return this.settle()
+     this.play(message.audio, message.text)
+   }
+ 
+   private play(audio: Float32Array, text: string): void {
+     const ctx = context()
+     if (!ctx || audio.length === 0) return
+     if (!this.out || !this.analyser) {
+       this.analyser = ctx.createAnalyser()
+       // Wide, so the lowest band is not one bin of a hundred hertz. The orb is
+       // read off this, and a bass band that never moves is an orb that only
+       // ever breathes at one end.
+       this.analyser.fftSize = 2048
+       this.analyser.smoothingTimeConstant = 0.72
+       this.out = ctx.createGain()
+       this.out.connect(this.analyser)
+       this.analyser.connect(ctx.destination)
+     }
+     const buffer = ctx.createBuffer(1, audio.length, SPEAK_RATE)
+     buffer.getChannelData(0).set(audio)
+     const source = ctx.createBufferSource()
+     source.buffer = buffer
+     source.connect(this.out)
+     const at = Math.max(ctx.currentTime + LEAD, this.nextAt)
+     const first = this.waiting === 0
+     this.waiting++
+     this.live.push(source)
+     source.onended = () => {
+       this.live = this.live.filter(held => held !== source)
+       this.waiting--
+       this.settle()
+     }
+     source.start(at)
+     this.nextAt = at + buffer.duration
+     if (first) globalThis.setTimeout(() => this.ears.onSaying(text), Math.max(0, (at - ctx.currentTime) * 1000))
+     else globalThis.setTimeout(() => this.ears.onSaying(text), Math.max(0, (at - ctx.currentTime) * 1000))
+   }
+ 
+   private settle(): void {
+     if (this.waiting > 0 || !this.sealed) return
+     this.nextAt = 0
+     this.ears.onQuiet()
+   }
+ }

Done. The plan is now a tab in the browser panel rather than a column of its own.

**How it behaves**
- It stands at the head of the tab row, wearing the checklist mark and the word Plan, and it opens on itself the moment you enter a thread that has one.
- It is not yours to close: no X on the pill, no close in its right-click menu, and `closeTab` refuses it even if something calls it. The panel's Close button takes the other tabs and leaves the plan standing, and while the plan is the only thing there the Close button is gone, since there is nothing left to close.
- It goes when you leave the thread. Only ever one plan, so opening another thread's takes the place of the one before it.
- Everything else in the panel is unchanged, so an agent opening a file mid-build gets its own pill and the plan is one press away again.

**What changed**
- `src/renderer/src/state/browser.ts` — a `plan` kind carrying its `threadId`, plus `showPlan`/`hidePlan`, and the two closes now leave it alone.
- `src/renderer/src/components/BrowserPanel.tsx` — the pill, the content, and one effect that follows the open thread.
- `src/renderer/src/components/PlanView.tsx` — the plan and the Implement plan button, replacing `PlanPanel.tsx`, which is deleted along with its line in `App.tsx`.
- `tests/plan-tab-probe.test.ts` — 8 tests covering all of the above. Green, along with `browser-tabs-probe`, `browser-image-probe` and `side-panel-resize-probe`.

One thing I dropped: the old header carried a `Not started` / `Building` pill. The Implement button already says the first and the thread says the second, so I left it out rather than spend a row on it. Say the word if you want it back.

Worth knowing, and not from this change: `plan-card-probe`, `thread-view-probe` and `huddle-probe` are all failing on main. I checked them against the commit before my edits and they fail there identically. Every one renders `App` and never gets past `Boot`, which holds 1.6 seconds on real timers. They need fake timers or reduced motion in their setup.

I'm noticing the `if (first)` conditional in `play` has duplicate branches that need to be removed. There's also a timing issue where `setTimeout` for captions isn't being cancelled when playback stops, so stale captions can appear after interruption. I need to track these timers and clear them in the `silence()` method, and I'm also seeing that both `settle()` and `stop()` are firing `onQuiet`, which might be creating redundancy since `stop()` calls `silence()` anyway.

The real issue is a race condition: if `seal()` is called while the worker is still sending chunks, `waiting` could briefly hit zero between arrivals and trigger `onQuiet` prematurely. I need to add a `finished` flag that the worker sets when it sends `done` for the current turn, so `settle()` only fires when both the worker is truly done AND there are no pending chunks.

I'm restructuring the state: initialize `finished = true` and `sealed = true`, then `seal()` sets `sealed = true` and tells the worker to close without calling settle immediately. When the worker sends `done`, it sets `finished = true` and calls `settle()`. The `settle()` check becomes: only fire `onQuiet` if `finished && waiting === 0`. This way, brief silences between sentences won't trigger the callback prematurely.

Rewriting mouth.ts cleanly now.

+ import { useCrew } from './state/store'
+ import { bootSeen, rememberBoot } from './components/boot/seen'
+ import Boot from './views/Boot'

+ import type { ListenIn, ListenOut } from './listen.worker'
+ 
+ export interface ListenerEars {
+   onFetching: (file: string, loaded: number, total: number) => void
+   onReady: () => void
+   onFailed: (message: string) => void
+ }
+ 
+ // Whisper, asked one utterance at a time. What comes back is only ever handed
+ // on if it is still the utterance being waited for: somebody who talks again
+ // while the last one is being read has changed their mind, and the older answer
+ // is a sentence from before that.
+ export class VoiceListener {
+   private worker: Worker | null = null
+   private next = 0
+   private waiting = new Map<number, (text: string) => void>()
+ 
+   constructor(private readonly ears: ListenerEars) {}
+ 
+   load(): void {
+     this.hire()?.postMessage({ type: 'load' } satisfies ListenIn)
+   }
+ 
+   hear(audio: Float32Array): Promise<string> {
+     const worker = this.hire()
+     if (!worker) return Promise.resolve('')
+     const id = ++this.next
+     return new Promise<string>(resolve => {
+       this.waiting.set(id, resolve)
+       worker.postMessage({ type: 'hear', id, audio } satisfies ListenIn, [audio.buffer])
+     })
+   }
+ 
+   // Everything still in flight comes back as nothing, so no caller is left
+   // holding a promise that will never settle.
+   forget(): void {
+     for (const resolve of this.waiting.values()) resolve('')
+     this.waiting.clear()
+   }
+ 
+   close(): void {
+     this.forget()
+     this.worker?.terminate()
+     this.worker = null
+   }
+ 
+   private hire(): Worker | null {
+     if (this.worker) return this.worker
+     if (typeof Worker === 'undefined') return null
+     const worker = new Worker(new URL('./listen.worker.ts', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })
+     worker.onmessage = (event: MessageEvent<ListenOut>) => this.heard(event.data)
+     this.worker = worker
+     return worker
+   }
+ 
+   private heard(message: ListenOut): void {
+     if (message.type === 'fetching') return this.ears.onFetching(message.file, message.loaded, message.total)
+     if (message.type === 'ready') return this.ears.onReady()
+     if (message.type === 'failed') {
+       if (message.id !== undefined) this.settle(message.id, '')
+       else this.ears.onFailed(message.message)
+       return
+     }
+     this.settle(message.id, message.text)
+   }
+ 
+   private settle(id: number, text: string): void {
+     const resolve = this.waiting.get(id)
+     if (!resolve) return
+     this.waiting.delete(id)
+     resolve(text)
+   }
+ }

metadata:

To judge Crew UI, render it and look at it. A throwaway vite build plus an Electron
`capturePage` shows a component at real panel sizes in a few seconds, which is far
quicker than launching the app and driving it to the screen in question.

Build a temp dir with `index.html`, a `main.tsx` that stubs `useCrew.setState({...})`
and renders the component at a fixed size, and a `probe.css`. **The css must be**

```css
@import "<repo>/src/renderer/src/styles.css";
@source "<repo>/src/renderer/src";
```

**Why:** Tailwind v4 detects content from the vite root. Importing `styles.css`
directly from a probe outside the repo compiles only the classes used in the probe
file itself, so the component renders completely unstyled and looks broken for a
reason that has nothing to do with the component. `@source` points the scan back at
the real tree.

**How to apply:** Put the probe under `node_modules/.<name>/` so nothing lands in
the auto-committing tree, `npx vite build --config <probe>/vite.config.ts`, then an
Electron main that `loadFile`s the built `dist/index.html`, waits ~1s and writes
`capturePage().toPNG()`. Delete the probe afterwards. Same shape as
`scripts/cover-sheet.mjs`, which is the committed version of this trick.
Related: [[crew-design-system]].

The voice gate is working as intended—it responds to speech, stays closed on hums, passes through gaps, drops on coughs, ignores clicks, and resists opening while the agent is speaking. Now I'm moving to the session state machine, which is the core piece. I'm defining a phase system that tracks the conversation flow through states like off, waking, listening, hearing, thinking, speaking, and trouble.

I'm building the state interface with properties for the current phase, thread and agent IDs, a progress indicator for loading, transcripts of what was heard and what's being said, voice cards, error handling, and mute/voice settings. The interface also includes methods to start and end sessions, control muting, change voices, and send typed responses.

For the flow, when starting a session I pick an agent, set the phase to waking, load both the mouth and listener, then open the ear once both are ready. When the ear detects speech, if the mouth is already speaking it interrupts and stops.

When the ear finishes capturing audio, I transition to thinking, convert the audio to text, and if there's actual content I send it to the thread and update the heard transcript. Then I watch the store for the agent's reply, streaming text steps into the mouth incrementally until the agent finishes. As the mouth speaks, I update the saying property and phase accordingly, returning to listening once it's quiet.

For subscribing to replies, I'm using the crew store which holds events and steps, watching for the agent to finish with our thread ID and monitoring the text steps as they stream in.

Now I need to understand how text steps accumulate their content during streaming — whether they build up the full text progressively or arrive in discrete pieces — so I can properly feed them into the text-to-speech system.

Looking at the rendered output, the card dimensions don't match what I'd expect—they're appearing around 265 CSS pixels wide when the stack should be 320, so I'm recalculating the actual measurements from the image coordinates to figure out what's going on with the layout.

The spacing checks out: the first card sits at about 78 CSS pixels from the top (70 for the header plus 8 padding), and the right edge has roughly 25 pixels of margin, which aligns with the right-24 class.

One thing I notice is that the plain toast without an icon has no indent, so its text starts flush at the left padding while the marked toasts have their text offset by the icon space—this creates a slightly ragged left edge, but it's acceptable since Sonner does the same thing and it still reads fine.

The real issue is the close button: when it's invisible on hover, the right side of the action button looks like it has excessive padding because the slot is being held but the button isn't visible. I could either accept this as-is or show the close button at low opacity all the time and brighten it on hover, which would make the spacing feel more intentional and honest about the reserved space.

There's a tension between keeping the interface quiet (hiding the dismiss affordance until needed) and making it discoverable and balanced. Most toast libraries either hide it completely or show it persistently—Sonner hides it, while macOS and Slack show it always. The question is whether the visual noise of a persistent close button on every row conflicts with the principle that every element should communicate something meaningful.

The best approach might be an absolutely positioned close button that appears on hover in the top-right corner, floating slightly outside the card's bounds. This avoids reserving layout space, prevents any shift on interaction, and keeps rows visually tight when idle—the button only materializes when you need it.

But there's a catch: the toast slot has `overflow: hidden`, which would clip a button positioned above the card's top edge. So the button needs to stay inside the bounds at `top-1.5 right-1.5`, though that risks overlapping text or an action button on two-line toasts. The compromise is keeping a reserved inline slot for the close icon, but rendering it at low opacity when idle and brightening it on row hover—this preserves the layout integrity while eliminating the visual hole.

I'm reconsidering whether the close button is even necessary since toasts auto-dismiss and actions handle user intent, but the ability to dismiss immediately when a toast blocks content is valuable enough to keep. I'll make it visible-but-quiet with this opacity approach and test both light and dark modes to ensure the marks and text remain legible.

The host accumulates text across steps, so each step carries the full text buffer up to that point, throttled by the flush interval. For streaming TTS, I'm tracking how much of each text step I've already sent to the mouth and only pushing the new portion since the last update—that way I avoid re-processing text I've already handled.

But there's a critical issue: I can't push partial text into the splitter if a card fence marker (```card ... ```) arrives later, because that would cause the voice to read out the JSON. The solution is to hold back text until it's safe—I need to identify the prefix that can't possibly be part of an incomplete card fence, and only push that. Since the TextSplitterStream already buffers until sentence boundaries, the real constraint is just avoiding pushing anything before a card fence is complete or stripped out.

I'm sketching out a helper function that computes what's safe to say so far by checking if any fence markers are open (odd number of ``` occurrences means a fence is still open), then cutting at that point. The tricky part is that transforming a fragment of text differently than the whole creates fragility when trying to diff against what's already been pushed. The cleanest approach is to compute the full spoken text from the safe raw content at each update, then only push the new portion that extends what was already said, checking that it starts with what we previously pushed to catch any edge cases where markdown resolved differently.

Actually, I'm realizing markdown transformations are mostly local and stable as text grows—like `**bold` stays unchanged until the closing `**` arrives, at which point it retroactively becomes `bold`. So the spoken text won't always be a pure extension. A safer strategy is to only push complete sentences from the safe raw text, since markdown pairs almost never straddle sentence boundaries. I'd track the raw length pushed so far, find the last sentence boundary in the safe text, and transform just that chunk (which is stable), then at seal time push whatever remains.

Rethinking the index tracking approach: instead of trying to match indices between raw and spoken text, I should just track the raw index and always transform the raw tail. On each update, I find the last sentence boundary in the safe text after the pushed index, transform that slice, and move the index forward. At finish, I compute the full spoken text from the final reply and extract the cards.

The key insight is treating newlines as sentence boundaries too, so card fences—which always start on their own line—never get split mid-fence. When I slice from the pushed index, I'm always working with complete raw text, and any terminated fence in the middle gets handled naturally by the transformation.

I'm thinking of this as a small, testable streaming reader module that collects both the spoken text and any cards that appear as chunks arrive, giving that live generative UI feel. I'll create a dedicated file for it—maybe `voiceReply.ts`—to keep things modular and focused.

Writing the VoiceReply class... I'm refining the boundary detection logic to avoid splitting on abbreviations like "e.g." or numbered lists. The key is checking that a period is followed by whitespace and that the character before it isn't a single letter, plus requiring at least a couple words before it counts as a sentence break. Newlines should always be treated as boundaries since they're unambiguous.

I'm not going to over-complicate this—the voice replies are typically just 1-3 sentences anyway, so the streaming benefit is modest. I'll implement the basic rule: boundaries are either after `[.!?]` followed by whitespace, or at newlines, with the abbreviation guard in place. + import { readReply, type VoiceCard } from './voice'
+ 
+ // A reply arrives a piece at a time and has to be spoken while it is still
+ // being written, or every answer waits for its own last word. Two things stop
+ // that being a plain hand-off of whatever just landed.
+ //
+ // A card is a fenced block, and half of one is a line of JSON. Nothing past an
+ // unclosed fence is ever handed over, so a card is either whole or not there.
+ //
+ // A sentence is the smallest thing worth saying. Handed "Let me check the" the
+ // voice says it with a full stop on the end and then starts again mid-clause,
+ // which is what a machine reading a teleprinter sounds like.
+ 
+ export interface Sayable {
+   say: string
+   cards: VoiceCard[]
+ }
+ 
+ const NOTHING: Sayable = { say: '', cards: [] }
+ 
+ const FENCE = /^[ \t]*```/gm
+ 
+ // A full stop after a single letter is an initial or an abbreviation, so "e.g."
+ // and "J. Smith" are not the end of anything.
+ const SENTENCE = /(?<![\s(][A-Za-z])[.!?…]["')\]]*(?=\s)/g
+ 
+ export function lastBoundary(text: string, from: number): number {
+   let end = from
+   const line = text.lastIndexOf('\n')
+   if (line >= from) end = line + 1
+   SENTENCE.lastIndex = from
+   for (let match = SENTENCE.exec(text); match; match = SENTENCE.exec(text)) {
+     const after = match.index + match[0].length
+     if (after > end) end = after
+   }
+   return end
+ }
+ 
+ export class VoiceReply {
+   private at = 0
+ 
+   // Everything that has become safe to say since the last time it was asked.
+   grew(raw: string): Sayable {
+     const fences = [...raw.matchAll(FENCE)]
+     const safe = fences.length % 2 === 0 ? raw : raw.slice(0, fences[fences.length - 1].index)
+     const end = lastBoundary(safe, this.at)
+     if (end <= this.at) return NOTHING
+     return this.take(safe.slice(this.at, end), end)
+   }
+ 
+   // The rest of it, once there is no more coming. Anything the sentence rule
+   // was still holding on to goes out here, whether or not it ends in a stop.
+   whole(raw: string): Sayable {
+     return this.at >= raw.length ? NOTHING : this.take(raw.slice(this.at), raw.length)
+   }
+ 
+   private take(chunk: string, to: number): Sayable {
+     this.at = to
+     const { spoken, cards } = readReply(chunk)
+     return { say: spoken, cards }
+   }
+ }
+

He's suggesting I could reduce the shadow intensity or increase the vertical gap to break up that effect. The `.glass` class is applying the full shadow, which might be too heavy for these small floating toast chips compared to the larger popovers it was designed for. I could override the shadow specifically on `.toast-card` to soften it while keeping the glass styling.
